gaps.why_it_matters: The stack research covered only SDK and target-API deadlines. The trends research cited Apple 5.3, 4.5.4 and 5.1.1(v). Nobody checked the rules that decide whether a money-moving app can be published at all, or under which account. Apple 5.1.1(ix) says apps in regulated financial services should be submitted by the legal entity that provides the service. Google Play requires an organization developer account and a Financial features declaration for financial apps, and some countries add their own requirements (India in particular). New personal Play accounts must also run a closed test with a minimum number of testers for a set period before production. Age-rating questionnaires and the 18+ gate, data-safety and privacy labels, and the account-deletion web link also matter. Any one of these can block a 'store-ready' release, or force a change to onboarding, the age gate, the Satellite paper-trading framing or Pay with Vaultwise. This changes the build and the release plan, not just polish.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: Vaultwise is a student capstone fintech prototype being turned into a native mobile app with Expo SDK 57 (React Native 0.86) for the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting adults 18+ (Gen Z) in the US, euro area, UK, India, Singapore, Canada, Australia and UAE. Features: purpose-locked savings 'vaults' (Health, Education, Housing, Emergency, Retirement, Custom) whose money is released only against an AI-verified invoice or receipt; tiered emergency withdrawals (PIN plus short hold); round-ups and auto-contribution rules that debit a linked bank; Core investing (index ETF SIP) and Satellite investing (paper trading only, labelled practice mode); an AI assistant (Groq LLM); joint vaults; and 'Pay with Vaultwise', where merchants integrate a checkout and the customer pays from a vault, with the merchant invoice verified at payment. Sign-in is by email with an in-app PIN and Face ID or fingerprint; Delete account is in Settings. Today is 2026-10-10. Task: find the CURRENT (2026) Apple App Review Guidelines and Google Play Developer Policy requirements that would block or reshape publishing this app, citing the primary-source URL for every claim (developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines, support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer, play.google.com/about/developer-content-policy). Cover: (1) Apple 5.1.1(ix) and related rules on regulated financial services: who must be the submitting entity, and whether an individual or student account can publish a savings, payments or investing app, a prototype or demo, or a 'simulated money' build. (2) Google Play's Financial Services policy and the Financial features declaration, the organization-account requirement for financial products, and the country-specific requirements for each of the 8 markets (especially India: RBI-related, personal-loan and UPI/payment rules; also the UK, Singapore, Australia and UAE). (3) The Google Play closed-testing requirement for new personal accounts (tester count and duration as of 2026) and identity and D-U-N-S verification. (4) Age ratings: Apple's current age-rating tiers and questionnaire, Play's target-audience and content settings, and what an 18+ fintech must declare. Note that Gen Z includes 14–17 year olds, who must be excluded. (5) Rules on simulated trading, paper trading or contests (Satellite), and on AI chat features (Apple's 2025–26 guidance on generative AI and third-party AI data sharing disclosure). (6) Payment rules for Pay with Vaultwise: confirm that paying merchants for physical goods or services from a vault falls outside IAP (Apple 3.1.3/3.1.5 and Play Payments policy), and any rules on NFC/HCE or QR in-store payments by region. (7) Account deletion (Apple 5.1.1(v), Play's deletion web-link requirement), Play Data safety, Apple privacy nutrition labels and Privacy Manifest required-reason APIs for Expo modules, and permission-rationale rules for camera and photos (Play Photo and Video Permissions policy). Output a table: requirement | applies to Vaultwise? (yes/no/conditional) | consequence for design or build | what the team must do | source URL. Clearly separate documented facts from your inference. Flag anything that makes public store release impossible for a student team, and propose the compliant fallback (for example TestFlight external testing or Play internal/closed testing only, a demo-mode build with no real money, or publishing under a university or organization account).

gaps.why_it_matters: The colour recommendation, Vault Violet as the signature hue, rests on a 23-app sample. Verification found it is effectively the same hue as PhonePe (#5F259F) and Jar in India, and the research's own BFA source says fintechs mostly use purple or blue. Pay with Vaultwise needs a checkout button and brand mark that merchants and customers can tell apart instantly, in all 8 markets. NN/g also argues against a dark-first default, and the dark-preference data could not be verified. The hue and the default theme feed every token, mockup, icon and the checkout identity, so getting them wrong means redoing the whole visual system.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: Vaultwise is a fintech mobile app (Expo/React Native) for Gen Z adults 18–29 in the US, euro area, UK, India, Singapore, Canada, Australia and UAE. It offers purpose-locked savings vaults, emergency access, investing and 'Pay with Vaultwise', a merchant checkout button and sheet where customers pay from a vault. Earlier research on 23 Gen Z apps found no single winning hue. The pattern was a black and white or greyscale base, one saturated signature accent kept for brand and primary actions, and a dark theme available (17 of 19). It proposed 'Vault Violet' #B688FE (dark mode) and #7A36D0 (light mode). Verification showed that hue ~300 collides with PhonePe #5F259F, and that the light violet is ΔE≈3 from Jar and ΔE≈9 from PhonePe. Fixed status colours are green, amber, red and blue. Today is 2026-10-10. Task A: build a colour-collision map of the signature brand colours of the major banks, neobanks, wallets, payment buttons and BNPL checkouts in each of the 8 markets. Include at least 8–12 per market, for example US: Chase, Cash App, Venmo, PayPal, Apple Pay, Zelle, Chime, SoFi, Klarna, Affirm, Afterpay; UK: Monzo, Revolut, Starling, Chase UK, Clearpay; India: PhonePe, Paytm, Google Pay, CRED, Jar, Jupiter, BHIM/UPI, Groww; Singapore: GrabPay, PayNow, DBS PayLah!, Trust; EU: N26, bunq, iDEAL, Wero, Satispay; Canada: Interac, Wealthsimple, KOHO; Australia: Up, CommBank, Zip, Afterpay; UAE: Liv, Wio, Careem Pay. Use each brand's official brand-guidelines or press-kit hex where possible, cite each URL, and mark sampled values as sampled. Convert to OKLCH and compute CIEDE2000 distances. Then propose 2–3 candidate signature hues (with dark and light variants) that sit at ΔE2000 ≥ 15 from every payment or checkout brand in those markets, avoid the status colours, show up strongly on near-black, and pass WCAG 2.2 contrast as text (4.5:1) and as non-text UI (3:1). Also check how each candidate reads under protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia. Note any cultural colour connotations in India, the UAE and Singapore, with sources. Task B: find primary evidence (2023–2026) on dark versus light default preference and readability for finance apps and Gen Z: NN/g articles on dark mode, peer-reviewed studies, platform data (Apple, Google, Android Authority, or a survey with a published method). Recommend default theme behaviour (follow system, dark default, or light default) with reasons. Output: the collision table, candidate palettes with computed contrast ratios (state the method), the theme-default recommendation, and a clear split between documented facts and inference.

gaps.why_it_matters: The user explicitly asked for haptics that feel satisfying 'like Opal'. The research found Opal has published almost nothing, and no one examined how Opal's haptics actually feel or are built. Verification also found that much of the 24-token haptic spec can't be built with expo-haptics 57.0.3 or react-native-pulsar 1.7.0. The missing pieces are prepare(), impact intensity, the GESTURE_THRESHOLD constants and scaled Android primitive compositions, and some API levels were wrong. So the build may need a custom Expo native module, which the spec treats only as a fallback. Without a feasibility map and an Opal benchmark, the haptics deliverable may be neither buildable nor the experience the user asked for.
gaps.research_prompt: Context: Vaultwise is a Gen Z fintech mobile app built with Expo SDK 57 (React Native 0.86.3, expo-haptics ~57.0.3) using development builds, not Expo Go. The user wants satisfying, science-backed haptics 'like Opal' (the Opal screen-time app, opal.so). A draft spec defines 24 named haptic tokens: PIN key tick, PIN success and failure, amount stepper detent, slider threshold, pull-to-refresh threshold, vault contribution 'locked', proof approved, proof routed to human review, declined, Tier-2 emergency hold start and countdown end, irreversible-action confirm (firm, distinct), milestone 25/50/100%, streak kept, and others. Payment success is deliberately neutral. There are Off, Subtle and Full intensity settings and device tiers. Today is 2026-10-10. Part 1, implementability: for each of these capabilities, determine with primary sources (npm package source on GitHub, Apple Core Haptics and UIFeedbackGenerator docs, Android Vibrator, VibrationEffect.Composition and HapticFeedbackConstants reference, Expo docs) whether it can be done from JavaScript with (a) expo-haptics 57.x, (b) react-native-pulsar 1.7.0 (read its README and native source: presets, custom patterns, AHAP or Core Haptics support, Android Composition support, amplitude scaling, the API levels it supports), (c) other maintained libraries such as react-native-haptic-feedback, or (d) only a custom Expo Modules API native module. Capabilities: transient intensity and sharpness on iOS; generator prepare and latency priming; continuous events; AHAP file playback; Android Composition primitives with per-primitive scale and delay (API 30/31+ availability checks via areAllPrimitivesSupported); performHapticFeedback constants including GESTURE_THRESHOLD_ACTIVATE/DEACTIVATE, SEGMENT_TICK and CONFIRM/REJECT (with exact API levels); amplitude-control detection; behaviour on Android battery saver and iOS Low Power Mode; respecting system touch-haptics settings. For each, cite the URL and give an estimate of the work for a custom Expo module if one is needed (for example a 150-line Swift and Kotlin module exposing playTransient(intensity, sharpness), playPattern(ahapJson) and playComposition([...])). Part 2, the Opal benchmark: find out what is publicly known about Opal's haptics and sensory design. Look at founder and designer posts (X/Twitter, LinkedIn, Medium, podcasts, Dribbble or Behance), App Store and Google Play review text mentioning haptic, vibration or 'feels', press and design write-ups, and Apple design award or feature coverage. If nothing documents it, say so plainly and describe a lawful observational method the team could use themselves on an iPhone and an Android flagship (for example recording accelerometer traces with a phone-on-phone method, or noting which interactions trigger feedback) to benchmark Opal and 2–3 other apps praised for haptics (for example Apple Wallet or Apple Pay, Robinhood, Duolingo, Revolut). Output: a feasibility matrix of token × library, a recommended architecture (which tokens use expo-haptics, Pulsar or a custom module), any Opal facts each with its own source URL, the benchmarking protocol, and a clear split between documented facts and inference.
